item.title: China issues 800 bln yuan via financial instruments to expand investment
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29 08:10:00
BUSINESS / ECONOMY China issues 800 bln yuan via financial instruments to expand investment By Xinhua Published: Oct 29, 2026 08:10 AM
China has completed the issuance of 800 billion yuan (about 119 billion U.S. dollars) under its 2026 new policy-based financial instruments as of Wednesday, channeling funds to key projects to expand effective investment, according to three policy banks. The China Development Bank allocated 365 billion yuan, involving projects with a total investment of 5.5 trillion yuan, and the Export-Import Bank of China allocated 120 billion yuan, helping leverage over 1.7 trillion yuan in investment, while the Agricultural Development Bank of China allocated 315 billion yuan, featuring projects with a total investment of around 4.39 trillion yuan. First launched in 2025 with an allocation of 500 billion yuan, these instruments prioritize the digital economy, artificial intelligence (AI), consumer infrastructure, and urban renewal endeavors such as transport, energy and underground pipe network upgrades. This year's government work report set the 2026 allocation at 800 billion yuan to attract more private capital. A large share of the funds went to AI and the digital economy. The China Development Bank allocated 179.01 billion yuan to projects in AI, the digital economy, green and low-carbon development, biomedicine and consumption. The Export-Import Bank of China supported more than 220 projects in emerging sectors like the digital economy and AI, with loans to these fields accounting for nearly half of its total allocation. The Agricultural Development Bank of China, meanwhile, supported almost 2,000 projects in areas including AI, the digital economy, the low-altitude economy, consumption and green and low-carbon development, with financing of nearly 200 billion yuan. Support for private investment was also strengthened. The China Development Bank allocated 127.99 billion yuan to projects involving private investment or private capital. The Export-Import Bank of China supported more than 210 such projects, accounting for almost 40 percent of its total allocation, while the Agricultural Development Bank of China supported nearly 400 projects with over 65 billion yuan. All of the 800 billion yuan was used to supplement project capital, helping ease capital shortages for major projects, improve their financing capacity, and leverage bank lending and private capital. Going forward, the three policy banks will strengthen post-investment management, provide supportive loans, and accelerate the conversion of funds into physical work to maximize the instruments' effectiveness. Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, said the rollout of 800 billion yuan via new policy-based financial instruments, together with major infrastructure projects and urban renewal initiatives, could stimulate demand for electronic information products, electrical machinery, high-end equipment and certain raw materials.

item.title: Why China's reaction to Mbappé's offensive remarks is not simply 'fervent nationalism'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29 00:16:00
Kylian Mbappé, a Real Madrid player in Spain's LaLiga Soon after French football star Kylian Mbappé's offensive remarks sparked widespread anger in China, some Western media outlets were quick to diagnose the Chinese public's reaction as "nationalism." Some Western commentators have dismissed the Chinese public's response as "oversensitivity" or "an inability to take a joke." NBC even claimed, "Mbappé is suddenly paying the penalty for being on the wrong side of China's fervent nationalism." Apparently, all it takes to make an insult acceptable is to label it a joke, and everyone else is expected to laugh along. The real divide lies in how different societies understand history, national dignity, and the line between humor and offense. Does that mean history can be freely mocked in the West, founding leaders can be turned into jokes, and anyone who objects is labeled a "fervent nationalist"? China's collective memory, shaped by a century of suffering, does not follow that logic. No country can tolerate attacks on its founding fathers; this is the most fundamental respect and norm in the international community. No society can tolerate its collective memory to be randomly insulted or joked about, even more so by a renowned celebrity. Expecting those who feel insulted to simply laugh it off is, in itself, a double standard. Chinese internet users do not expect Mbappé to become a Chinese historian, nor do they demand that a football star in his 20s agree with every Chinese political position. But he is not just another young man. He is a global superstar who benefits significantly from the Chinese market and enjoys the support of Chinese fans. Precisely because of this, he cannot simply ignore the historical memory and cultural sensibilities of the Chinese public. If humor is defined solely by the side doing the offending, and those who feel offended must first pass an ideological test before they can object, then this is not humor. It is a double standard dressed up as a joke. The real question is not why the Chinese public reacted so strongly, but why some Western media outlets were so quick to label that reaction "fervent nationalism." Why are they using the controversy as an opportunity to reinforce the claim that China is somehow incapable of taking a joke in the way the West supposedly can? That line of thinking raises a deeper question: What have Western education systems and media taught their audiences about China's history and its present-day realities? And what kind of image of China have they been creating? When a so-called joke can casually trample on another country's founding leader while those who object are the ones blamed, the real distortion is not the Chinese reaction; it is the arrogance that one side gets to decide what counts as a joke and what counts as an insult.

item.title: Hello Kitty should not dance with Japan's right wing: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29 00:03:00
The view of Sanrio Gift Gate, an officially licensed Sanrio merchandise store, in Wuhan, Central China's Hubei Province, on March 2, 2026. Photo: VCG Pop culture is a key industry in Japan, with manga, TV series, and other works attracting a large international audience. Consequently, it has become a "prime target" for Japan's right-wing forces. Sanrio's core audience includes a large number of adolescents and young consumers. Whether out of its pacifist values or its social responsibility to protect young people, the company must draw a clear line against distorted historical views. News that Sanrio, the Japanese company behind iconic IPs including Hello Kitty, Cinnamoroll, and My Melody, is launching co-branded merchandise tied to VIVANT , a Japanese drama notorious for smearing China, has sparked shock and fierce backlash on social media. According to official previews for VIVANT , following the "initial release" of plush toys in July this year featuring Hello Kitty, My Melody and other characters dressed as the show's "spy figures," the second batch of products from this collaboration has been approved for release. Details such as the launch date, product lineup and pricing have yet to be disclosed. VIVANT is no ordinary Japanese drama. Under the guise of a "spy thriller," it deliberately distorts the truth and reverses black and white, portraying the atrocities committed by the invading Japanese army against the Chinese people as actions of the Chinese side. The series was condemned by Chinese media for "packaging aggressive narratives through cognitive and information warfare," drawing widespread criticism. The content and ideology of this series reflect the historical outlook and anti-China narrative of the current conservative Japanese right-wing administration, catering to the trend of right-wing extremism in Japanese society; its motives and objectives are both deeply sinister. The commercial tie-in of Sanrio, beloved by audiences for its cartoon characters, with this confrontational drama that peddles biased narratives runs starkly counter to the "cute" and "healing" image its IPs have long embodied. It undermines the emotional bond and commercial credibility that its IPs have built among Chinese fans. The global popularity of Sanrio's IPs is closely tied to its founder's philosophy of peace. Shintaro Tsuji, the company's founder, personally experienced the Kofu Air Raid in World War II. After witnessing the harm inflicted on civilians by the ravages of war, he resolved to make "everyone get along together in harmony" the company's philosophy, aiming to promote cross-cultural peace through small gifts that convey smiles and goodwill. The company name "Sanrio" is derived from the Spanish phrase meaning "Saint River," expressing the hope that, just as rivers nurture civilization, the company would foster understanding rather than division among people. Hello Kitty's mouthless design symbolizes listening and mutual support and has long been interpreted as a symbol of friendship. It is precisely for this reason that Sanrio's "lapse" is all the more regrettable. Pop culture is a key industry in Japan, with manga, TV series, and other works attracting a large international audience. Consequently, it has become a "prime target" for Japan's right-wing forces. Japan's "Defense White Paper," released in August, featured a manga-style cover for the first time, linking the expansion of the military-industrial complex to "national prosperity" - a move that drew strong criticism from all quarters for its intent to poison and mislead young people. Sanrio's core audience includes a large number of adolescents and young consumers. Whether out of its pacifist values or its social responsibility to protect young people, the company must draw a clear line against distorted historical views. China is an indispensable overseas market for Sanrio. In the first half of 2026, its revenue generated from the Chinese market hit 781 million yuan ($117 million), surging more than 40 percent year-on-year. The group has previously stated its ambition to nurture its next breakout IP, on par with Cinnamoroll, within the Chinese market. If it values the Chinese market, Sanrio must translate respect for China into concrete actions. After news of this collaboration broke, a huge number of social media users made it clear that they "cannot accept it." Sanrio needs to understand that if the brand "partners with anti-China content," it stands to lose far more than short-term sales. The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer. When it comes to historical perceptions, Sanrio must not play with fire alongside Japan's right wing. Even more alarming is the fact that in recent years, Japanese society has seen a surge in popular cultural works that package war crimes as rousing tales. For example, the film The Eternal Zero , which centers on the Kamikaze special attack units, was widely criticized for romanticizing the image of the kamikaze pilots and downplaying Japan's responsibility as the aggressor. The anime My Hero Academia named one of its villains "Maruta" - a derogatory term used by Unit 731 of the Japanese Imperial Army to refer to victims of human experimentation during the invasion of China - thereby confirming its attempt to sneak in a hidden agenda. The Japanese fashion brand WEGO, which had partnered with the anime, also faced widespread boycotts. Sanrio is not the first to be tainted by this, nor will it be the last. China has always welcomed foreign brands with an open attitude. Over the years, many multinational companies have established a firm foothold in the Chinese market precisely because of their respect for Chinese consumers and China's history and culture. We are not asking Sanrio to take sides between China and Japan. Rather, we hope it makes a right choice on a fundamental issue: to partner with works that convey sound values and, above all, uphold a correct understanding of history. The concept of "everyone getting along together in harmony" cannot remain merely a slogan behind cute cartoon characters. It must be reflected in consistent commitment to peace and a firm refusal to appease or indulge right-wing agitation. Sanrio has both the duty and urgency to make its stance clear.

item.title: China's independently developed super-large-diameter shield machine is powering through the world's longest undersea high-speed railway tunnel
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 23:08:00
A view of the excavation point where China's domestically built, super-large-diameter shield machine, "Yongzhou," operates in Ningbo, East China's Zhejiang Province, in September Photos on this page: Courtesy of China Railway 14th Bureau Group Every day, the smartphone of Dong Bing, the chief mechanical engineer of Yongzhou Railway project, buzzes with messages from a machine working deep beneath the seabed. The real-time push notifications track almost every aspect of the operation of "Yongzhou," a 135-meter-long, domestically built super-large-diameter shield machine. Whether the cutterhead torque is abnormal, the segments are floating or the main drive oil and seal pressures remain within the safe range all determine whether the multi-thousand-ton "steel giant" can advance safely beneath the seabed. "This tunnel boring machine's (TBM) intelligent system is more sensitive than people," Dong told the Global Times on the way to the machine's latest excavation point. "Some problems are impossible to catch by human inspection. You walk past and everything looks fine. Then, a second later, a problem appears. The system can also pull the data together, identify related conditions and analyze possible causes. That is a huge help for safety," he explained. Far beneath the sea, "Yongzhou" is approaching one of the most demanding stages of its journey. Having advanced more than 4,000 meters from the Ningbo side, the machine has completed about 83 percent of its planned excavation and is heading toward the deepest section, about 93 meters beneath the seabed. After passing that point, it will meet another giant TBM "Dinghai," advancing from the opposite direction on the Zhoushan side, at the designated underwater docking point. The two machines will eventually achieve a precise rendezvous beneath the seabed, before being dismantled inside the completed tunnel. Their destination is part of the Jintang undersea tunnel, a key section of the Yongzhou Railway that connects Ningbo and Zhoushan in East China's Zhejiang Province. Stretching 16.18 kilometers in total, with an 11.21-kilometer shield-driven section, it is the world's longest undersea high-speed railway tunnel. The project sets multiple world records: it is the undersea high-speed railway shield tunnel with the highest water and earth pressure, the most complex geology and the greatest construction difficulty. But the significance of this engineering feat extends beyond the tunnel itself. Once heavily dependent on imported shield machines, China has now become the world's largest market and producer of these machines. And an on-site visit to "Yongzhou" offers a window into a broader transformation of Chinese high-end manufacturing - from "relying on imports" to "being able to build" to "building intelligently," and from scattered domestic breakthroughs to an integrated innovation capability that combines independent design, core manufacturing, intelligent construction and global engineering services. Gnawing through undersea 'ribs' Near the TBM's latest excavation point, the Global Times reporter saw cutters that had just been removed from the machine. Some bore deep grooves and flattened edges. Others had chunks missing from their cutting rings, while still others had been worn down almost beyond recognition. To date, about 4,000 cutters have been replaced. Dong said that the machine is expected to reach the deepest section by the end of this year. The closer it gets, the more complex the geological conditions become, the tougher the excavation becomes. Previously, the machine needed roughly one cutter replacement for every meter of advance. Now, Dong explained, a cutter may need to be replaced after just a few dozen centimeters. "If excavating through ordinary soil is like eating a meat-filled bun, then working here is like eating a bun filled with ribs. You not only have to deal with the 'meat' inside, but also gnaw through the hard 'bones' bit by bit," Dong said, using an analogy from everyday life. Along the Ningbo side route, the machine must navigate eight sections of full-face hard rock, 12 sections of mixed upper-soft and lower-hard strata and four sections of full-face soft soil. Nearly 70 percent of the route consists of unfavorable ground conditions, with rock strength reaching as high as 240 megapascals - more than eight times that of ordinary concrete. In some sections, the cutterhead must simultaneously deal with soft soil and extremely hard rock - posing another challenge. In such a context, the China Railway 14th Bureau Group tailored the "Yongzhou" TBM for these conditions. It has an excavation diameter of 14.57 meters and is equipped with 308 cutters on its cutterhead. The TBM was put into operation in May 2024. TBM operators work at the operator cab of "Yongzhou" in Ningbo, East China's Zhejiang Province, in September. Becoming 'smarter' The innovations on "Yongzhou" - ranging from undersea "space station," to remote driving and artificial intelligence (AI) models - all demonstrated a new direction for Chinese TBM technology: not only making the machines bigger and stronger, but also making them smarter and more efficient. When the Global Times reporter visited "Yongzhou" last week, the TBM was in the middle of another intensive round of cutter replacement. Unlike conventional pressurized entry techniques, which limit workers' effective working time to as little as 40 minutes a day under high pressure, the "Deep Sea Space Station" - China's first independently developed saturation-pressure intervention system for shield tunneling - allows technicians to remain in a pressurized living chamber and work in shifts over up to 28 days. Dong could still vividly recall the station's first application in February, when nine professional saturation divers, divided into three groups, carried out a 22-day operation at a depth of approximately 75 meters, replacing 46 cutters in total. "I was under tremendous pressure, but at the same time, I felt excited because we're advancing a very revolutionary innovation. Once we are successful, the homegrown innovation will fill a domestic technical gap, helping tackle one of the most challenging aspects of deep undersea tunneling while also accumulating valuable experience and technical reserves for future long-distance tunnels built under high water pressure," Dong said. The equipment has a maximum operating depth of 200 meters. And to date, it has successively completed cutter replacement tasks at 75 meters and 80 meters beneath the seabed. Another intelligent push Dong's team is pioneering is a remote-driving platform, also the first-of-its-kind application for a large-diameter TBM. "With manned supervision onboard, a TBM operator can now sit at the ground control center, about four kilometers from the excavation point, and control the machine as it advances underground - a sharp transformation from traditional construction, in which operators must work inside the machine deep underground," said Cheng Jie, assistant TBM operator. Making such remote operations possible is a sophisticated smart digital system that acts as the TBM's "eyes and ears" deep beneath the seabed. Through cameras and sensors, the system continuously tracks the cutterhead's operating conditions, cutter wear and key excavation parameters, while analyzing the data to detect potential abnormalities. When something unusual occurs, it can send real-time alerts directly to the phones of key engineers, including Dong, allowing them to identify risks and make informed decisions. According to Cheng, the next step is moving toward intelligent operation. "In the future, operators may only need to issue a start command, and the TBM will automatically activate its propulsion system according to preset parameters," she said, highlighting the technology as an important preparation for construction in hazardous environments and emergency situations. "The next generation of Chinese TBMs will move toward greater sophistication, intelligence and environmental sustainability," said Hao Weiqi, deputy director of the office of the High-end Equipment Industry Technology Research Institute under China Railway Construction Corp. The research institute has been focusing on intelligent excavation, digital twins and remote monitoring to enable underground construction with fewer workers or even unmanned operations. Besides, by integrating with AI, simulation technologies and digital twins, Chinese companies are moving beyond supplying individual TBMs toward providing comprehensive underground engineering solutions. A view of the excavation point where "Yongzhou" operates in Ningbo, East China's Zhejiang Province, in September The 'king of engineering machinery' TBM, known as the "king of engineering machinery," is a hallmark of high-end equipment. Chinese-made full-face TBMs now account for more than two-thirds of the global market and over 95 percent of China's domestic market for new machines, according to industry data. The Global Times learned from China Railway Construction Heavy Industry Corp that the company's TBMs have been exported to more than 30 countries and regions, including Türkiye, South Korea, Italy, Zambia, Peru and Romania. "Chinese companies' core advantage is the ability to customize equipment for different geological conditions compared with other foreign peers. We can tailor machines to specific underground environments while providing integrated solutions that combine equipment, intelligent systems and technical services throughout the entire construction process, backed by rapid delivery and response," Hao said. The growing global competitiveness was a sharp contrast to the scene a few decades ago, when China's underground construction projects depended heavily on foreign-made TBMs. Those machines were expensive to purchase, while maintenance and repairs were often constrained by overseas suppliers, Dong recalled. "It is through continuous efforts by Chinese enterprises, based on the on-site needs of major projects, that they have continuously tackled key challenges and gradually achieved domestic substitution, moving from imitation and catching up to independent innovation and partial leadership," Hao said. China has also achieved technological self-reliance in key TBM components, including cutterheads, cutters, main drives, an 8.61-meter integral ultra-large-diameter main bearing, intelligent numerical control systems and seals, overcoming multiple technological bottlenecks, Hao added. Across the country, homegrown TBMs have been deployed in an increasingly wide range of tunneling projects, navigating complex geological conditions beneath rivers, lakes, seas, mountains and cities. Among them, the "Linghang," the world's largest-diameter shield machine designed for high-speed railway tunneling, has successfully passed beneath the Yangtze River, while the "Shenjiang-1" also set a record for underwater shield excavation at a depth of 113 meters beneath the seabed. The Yongzhou Railway, where "Yongzhou" is currently operating, is expected to open to traffic in 2028. By then, the high-speed rail journey from Ningbo to Zhoushan will take only 26 minutes, ending Zhoushan's history of having no railway connection. "We're now so close to the rail industry's dream of crossing the strait," Dong said, as the massive machine continued its journey deep beneath the seabed.

item.title: Chinese team finds 3 new planets, prompting new questions about Earth's future
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 22:34:00
Photo: Courtesy of Qian Shengbang Chinese scientists have discovered three exoplanets that challenge the existing understanding of how planets evolve around aging stars, the research team behind the discoveries told the Global Times on Wednesday. Like the sun, most stars generate light and heat by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. When their core hydrogen is exhausted, they eventually expand dramatically into red giants, potentially growing to hundreds of thousands or even millions of times their original volume. Nearby planets then face a grim fate: They may be directly engulfed by the stars' expanding atmospheres or gradually pulled toward them by tidal forces until they eventually plunge into the stars, said Qian Shengbang, a professor at the School of Physics and Astronomy at Yunnan University and head of the research team. However, the team has identified three exoplanets that appear to have survived in what current models predict to be a danger zone. The researchers confirmed that the three host stars have entered the core helium-burning phase after passing through the red giant phase, during which their planets would have been expected to be engulfed at their present orbital distances. The findings reveal a "survival paradox" that challenges current models of stellar and planetary evolution. The discovery of multiple examples suggests that the phenomenon may not be an isolated case and warrants further investigation into possible underlying physical mechanisms, said the team. "If we had found only one surviving planet in the past, we could still have explained it as a chance occurrence. But finding three 'lucky survivors' at once suggests that this is not an isolated case and that there may be some underlying physical mechanism common to all of them," Qian said. The discovery also raises intriguing questions about the future of our own solar system. In several billion years, the sun is expected to enter its red giant phase. Traditional theories suggest that Earth will most likely be engulfed by the expanding sun, but the new findings highlight the complexity of interactions between aging stars and their planets, potentially offering new insights into planetary survival, although they do not directly change current predictions about Earth's fate, Qian said. The team first analyzed subtle changes in the brightness of the three exoplanets' host stars - 24 Boo, HD 12648 and TYC 4282-605-1 - using satellite data and asteroseismology, confirming that the stars had entered the core helium-burning stage. Among them, exoplanet 24 Boo b orbits its host star roughly once every 30 days, at an orbital distance of just 18 percent of the distance between the Earth and the sun. It is the closest known exoplanet orbiting a red clump giant star, the team said. The team then used models to reconstruct how far the three stars had expanded during their past evolution and compared these estimates with the planets' current orbits. The results showed that all three planets orbit within the regions where they were theoretically expected to have been engulfed by their host stars. Yet all three have survived and remain in existence. The new findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences as "The Survival Paradox of Close-In Planets Orbiting Red Clump Giants," according to the team.

item.title: Liaoning carrier group expands operations in western Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 22:28:00
Photo: CCTV China's Liaoning aircraft carrier group is conducting far-seas training in the western Pacific, while Japan has reported sightings of over a dozen Chinese naval vessels in the region, including at least four Type 055 large destroyers. Chinese experts say the formidable lineup highlights the Chinese navy's growing capabilities for long-range operations. On Wednesday, Japan reported Chinese vessel activities in the region, including a Type 055 destroyer, a Type 052D destroyer, a Type 054A frigate and a China Coast Guard vessel. The latest reports bring the total number of Chinese naval and coast guard vessels identified in the region in recent weeks to at least 17. One day earlier, Japan's Defense Ministry Joint Staff said in a release that it had spotted two Chinese naval vessels, a destroyer with hull number 117 and a frigate with hull number 546, west of Kume Island in the Okinawa Prefecture at around 10 am that day. The vessels subsequently sailed southeast between Okinawa's main island and Miyako Island toward the Pacific Ocean. A separate release by Japan on the same day said it had spotted another group of Chinese warships, including a destroyer with hull number 102 and a replenishment ship with hull number 903 heading in the same direction. The latest sightings followed a series of releases by Japan's defense ministry earlier in October concerning Chinese naval movements in the western Pacific. The movements came after the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy announced on October 14 that a carrier task group led by the Liaoning had set out to the western Pacific for training. The exercises are part of the PLA Navy's annual training plan and are intended to test and improve the troops' combat-oriented training capabilities and their ability to fulfill missions, according to the announcement. The training complies with relevant international law and practices and is not directed at any specific country or target, the navy said. The carrier group's movements have also drawn attention from the Philippines. The Armed Forces of the Philippines' Western Mindanao Command claimed that its maritime units tracked the Liaoning task group passing through waters off the Zamboanga Peninsula on October 22, according to Philippine media outlet INQUIRER.net. The report said the fleet was initially spotted northwest of Talulu Point in Siocon, Zamboanga del Norte, before being seen southwest of Maitum, Sarangani, as it moved southeast toward the Celebes Sea. The passage may mark the second time the Liaoning has transited the central Philippine maritime region, following a similar passage in 2024. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times that the lineup for this deployment is particularly formidable, describing it as a "high-end configuration" of a carrier battle group. He said aircraft carrier formations are complex, carefully designed systems whose composition varies depending on operational plans and mission requirements. In his view, the Type 055 destroyer is expected to become a central component of China's naval operations in distant waters, particularly in escorting aircraft carrier groups. China has 10 Type 055 destroyers in service - eight from a first batch and two from a second batch - with more expected to enter service, Song said. The Type 055 builds on the technological foundation of the Type 052D destroyer but features larger displacement and enhanced combat and logistical support capabilities, Song said. He described the Type 052D as a mainstay model, with some of its missions potentially being taken over by the Type 055 as the latter becomes more widely deployed. The Type 055's primary role in a carrier battle group is to provide outer-perimeter protection, including area air defense and anti-submarine defense, while it also possesses the capability to strike surface and land targets, Song said. The Type 052D will continue to perform combat and support missions in China's near and distant seas, while the Type 055 could take on a greater role in operations farther from China's shores, potentially including escort missions in the Gulf of Aden, he said. "In a word, China's overall naval combat capabilities, including its ability to operate and provide support in distant seas and airspace, are growing significantly," noted Song. Aircraft carriers remain the principal offensive component of carrier battle groups, with their embarked aircraft capable of establishing air superiority and conducting strikes against maritime and land targets at ranges beyond those covered by the ships themselves, he noted. The types of carrier-based aircraft accompanying the Liaoning on its deployment to the western Pacific have also drawn widespread public attention. Following the Liaoning group's return to its home port in June after more than 40 days of a previous far-seas combat-oriented training, footage was released publicly for the first time showing multiple J-15T carrier-based fighter jets taking off from and landing on the carrier, state broadcaster CCTV News reported. The J-15T is a domestically developed, single-seat, heavy carrier-based fighter designed for catapult-assisted takeoff. Based on the J-15, also known as the Flying Shark, the upgraded model features improvements to its avionics, weapons systems and airframe, with enhanced capabilities for carrier operations and maritime adaptability. According to Song, together with attack submarines, replenishment ships and land-based early-warning aircraft, the carrier and its escort vessels form an integrated combat system. Meanwhile, submarines can help counter underwater threats and strike surface and land targets, while replenishment ships provide fuel, ammunition and other supplies needed for sustained operations. The combination of carrier-based aircraft, large destroyers and supporting vessels enables the Chinese navy to conduct more complex operations across distant seas and airspace, Song said.

item.title: China's agricultural drone fleet exceeds 300,000 units, ranking first in the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 21:52:00
A worker operates two large agricultural drones to spray cornfields for pest and disease control at Gangbu Farm in Lianyungang, East China's Jiangsu Province, on August 5, 2026. Local farmers are using mechanized and high-tech methods to manage autumn crops, including rice, soybeans and corn, helping ensure stable yields and increase grain output. Photo: VCG China operates the world's largest fleet of agricultural drones, with more than 300,000 covering more than 460 million mu (30.67 million hectares) of farmland every year, CCTV News reported on Wednesday. Once used mainly for crop spraying, the aircraft are now deployed to monitor crop conditions and transport agricultural supplies and harvested products. Compared with manual labor, plant-protection drones can improve operational efficiency by more than 20 times, while reducing water use by more than 50 percent and cutting pesticide consumption by 20 percent to 40 percent, industry data showed. Agricultural drones have become the main type of technical equipment used in crop protection work across China. With drones and robots leading the way, smart agricultural machines are expanding into ever more diverse applications, boosting agricultural yields across the country. Industry experts said that low-altitude equipment is shifting from an "experimental novelty" to a standard feature of specialized agricultural services, becoming an important force for reducing costs, improving efficiency and promoting the upgrading of China's agriculture sector. According to CCTV News, the applications for drones in agriculture are also expanding rapidly. Tasks once done by hand such as watering water bamboo, transporting oranges down mountains and carrying out field inspections are increasingly handled by low-altitude equipment, fundamentally reducing labor costs in farming. In Guan'ao Village in Huangyan district of Taizhou, East China's Zhejiang Province, a local cooperative has adopted drones for routine farm work. Using drones, the cooperative can complete spraying and fertilizing across 500 mu of water bamboo fields in a single day. Each spraying session saves about 5,000 yuan ($749.96) to 6,000 yuan, while annual labor savings amount to 30,000 to 40,000 yuan. Zhou Li, a professor at the School of Agricultural Economics and Rural Development at Renmin University of China, told the Global Times that the rapid spread of agricultural drones in China is being driven by several factors. First, urbanization has changed the rural labor structure, raising farm wages and intensifying the demand for machines that can replace manual labor. Second, policy support for the low-altitude economy has accelerated the sector's development, with agriculture becoming one of its most mature commercial applications. Third, domestic manufacturers have continued to improve drone technology while reducing costs, making the devices more accessible to small farmers and cooperatives, Zhou noted. According to Zhou, drones are useful beyond crop protection. As orchards, tea plantations and protected cultivation expand, drones are showing clear advantages in hilly and mountainous areas and in scattered plots that are difficult for large machinery to reach. Their increasing use in transport, pollination, seed spreading and field monitoring suggests the market still has significant potential. In addition, experts said that the increasing intelligence of drones is fostering agricultural social services and creating new job opportunities. Agricultural drones are only one example of China's broader push toward smart farming. In recent years, the country has accelerated the digital and intelligent transformation of agriculture, with a wide range of smart devices playing an increasingly important role in production. According to domestic media reports, technologies such as smart harvesting robots, intelligent irrigation systems, and artificial intelligence-powered laser weeding robots are beginning to be deployed in agricultural operations, further enhancing efficiency and precision across the industry. China made significant progress in agricultural mechanization during the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-25) period. According to an official of the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, the contribution rate of agricultural science and technology progress exceeded 64 percent, the coverage rate of improved crop varieties surpassed 96 percent, and the comprehensive mechanization rate for crop planting, management and harvesting reached 76.7 percent, with major grain crops now largely fully mechanized. item.title: GT Voice: Caterpillar's legal fight exposes paradox of Western protectionism against China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 21:44:00
A worker assembles a tractor at a manufacturing plant in Caterpillar Industrial Park in Qingzhou, East China's Shandong Province, on September 27, 2026. Photo: VCG US manufacturer Caterpillar's legal challenge against the UK's trade watchdog lays bare an often-overlooked fact about Western trade protectionism: When the West targets "Chinese-made goods," the real casualties may include multinational companies long intertwined with Chinese supply chains. Caterpillar, the world's largest maker of construction equipment, is fighting to overturn an 18.81 percent anti-dumping duty that the UK's Trade Remedies Authority (TRA) has imposed on its China-built excavators, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday. The investigation was launched by the UK following a complaint from British equipment producer JCB, which complained that excavators from China were being sold in the UK "at unrealistically low prices." But Caterpillar contends that the TRA applied flawed logic when it imposed the duty, as its UK export prices for the excavators were higher than domestic prices in China, the report said. Whatever the outcome of the case, the fact that an American giant has to go to court to fight a tariff imposed by an ally has laid bare the misalignment of the entire trade protection mechanism. Some Western politicians have reduced trade disputes to a contest between countries and ideological blocs, deliberately ignoring a well-established reality: Global supply chains are deeply intertwined. After decades of integration driven by globalization, the ties between foreign investors and China's supply chains run far deeper than many political circles care to acknowledge. From 2020 to 2024, China's total industrial added value grew from 31.3 trillion yuan ($4.4 trillion) to 40.5 trillion yuan, while manufacturing added value increased from 26.6 trillion yuan to 33.6 trillion yuan. Chinese manufacturing accounts for nearly 30 percent of the global total, and among 504 major industrial products worldwide, China ranks first in output for the majority. Behind a single piece of construction machinery lies the coordinated operation of hundreds of component suppliers, skilled workers, nationwide logistics networks and large-scale manufacturing capabilities. Moreover, multinational corporations do not set up facilities in China merely to chase low costs. Their core motivation is to access the industrial clusters built up over decades and complete supporting systems that no other market can easily replicate. The choices of multinational corporations offer the most straightforward illustration of these deep industrial connections. In a 2026 survey by the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, 75 percent of European companies said that their production efficiency in China outpaced that in other regions. During the first nine months of this year, more than 47,000 foreign-invested enterprises were newly established in China. Foreign companies showed greater willingness to reinvest their profits in China. Reinvestment reached 93.99 billion yuan, up 4.7 percent year-on-year, with the growth rate expanding 1.5 percentage points compared with the previous year. New reinvestment projects continued to emerge in high-tech sectors, including artificial intelligence and biomedicine. These figures show that China is no longer just a sales market - it has become a critical hub for procurement, manufacturing and innovation in the global networks of countless multinational corporations. When multinationals deploy production capacity in China, what they value has never been the "unfair subsidies" of certain Western narratives, but the full-chain efficiency advantage brought by China's industrial clusters, a hard-earned outcome of decades of the global division of labor and cooperation. Such supply-chain advantages do not constitute dumping. Multinational corporations know their operational realities, and they understand the true costs of arbitrary trade barriers better than most. That reality gives them every incentive to step forward and share what operating in China is really like. The much-hyped "dumping" narratives are essentially little more than fig leaves for declining domestic industries trying to dodge fair market competition through protectionist measures. Rather than let such false narratives spread, the voices grounded in real business operations deserve to be amplified. That, in itself, is a powerful rebuttal to trade protectionism.

item.title: China steps up efforts to boost EU inbound travel
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 21:44:00
Zhangjiajie National Forest Park in central China's Hunan Province on October 23, 2026, draws a steady stream of visitors from around the world. Overseas ticket purchases for the park have exceeded 1 million so far this year, up more than 40 percent year on year, with visitors coming from 190 countries and regions worldwide—a record high. Photo: VCG In a fresh bid to reinvigorate inbound tourism from Europe, the Mission of China to the EU unveiled a campaign at Brussels Airport on Tuesday (Belgian time), shining a spotlight on streamlined entry for visitors from 25 EU member states. The move underscores the momentum behind two-way travel between China and Europe - flows that are already substantial in both directions and still gathering pace. The four-week campaign brings images of China to the airport's departure areas. It puts visa facilitation at the center of efforts to encourage travel and strengthen connections between China and Europe, industry media outlet Travel Tomorrow reported. Speaking at the inauguration, Eduardo Santander, CEO of the European Travel Commission, said that he hoped China's visa-free policy would encourage more Europeans to visit the country. A regular visitor himself, he highlighted the convenience of the arrangements and expressed hope that Europe would eventually be able to reciprocate by facilitating travel for Chinese visitors, the report said. European arrivals have grown steadily since China eased its visa-free policy, with year-on-year growth holding at 15-20 percent over the past two years and source markets such as Germany performing especially well, Xu Xiaolei, a marketing manager at CYTS Tours Holding Co, told the Global Times on Wednesday. "A deeper shift is underway in how they travel. Group tours are losing ground to independent and backpacking trips, and the itineraries now reach well beyond first-tier cities. Increasingly, European visitors want to wander through neighborhood streets and soak up local life, experience traditional Chinese medicine and other heritage practices, and buy Chinese consumer tech," Xu said. Germany is among the strongest-performing source markets, and cultural ties are being reinforced at the highest level. On Wednesday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier visited Hongcun, a UNESCO World Heritage village, and the Huangshan Mountain in East China's Anhui Province. Later in Beijing, he will visit the Summer Palace, the Guardian Art Center and the People's Art Theatre, according to the German President's official website. "Steinmeier's route through Anhui and Beijing reads like a checklist of shared interests: conserving World Heritage, interpreting it for visitors, marketing destinations abroad and developing experience-driven tourism - a reminder of the considerable potential between China and Germany and even China and the EU in terms of tourism cooperation," Song Wei, a professor at the School of International Relations and Diplomacy at Beijing Foreign Studies University, told the Global Times on Wednesday. China began introducing its unilateral visa-free initiative in December 2023, initially offering stays of up to 15 days to citizens of France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Malaysia. The policy subsequently expanded to additional countries, including Switzerland, Hungary and Belgium in March 2024, and the permitted stay increased to 30 days in November 2024. On October 15 and 16, Peter Tschentscher, mayor of Hamburg, Germany, led a delegation of government, business and academic representatives to Shanghai, as the two cities marked 40 years of friendship, according to the Shanghai government's website. The two sides conducted exchanges in aspects including green shipping, technological innovation, and culture and tourism. During a visit to China Eastern Airlines, Tschentscher expressed hope that direct flights between Shanghai and Hamburg could be introduced. He said that an air link would facilitate travel and strengthen business, cultural and tourism exchanges. China and the EU are highly complementary economically with deep convergence of interests, providing practical foundations for the two sides to deepen cooperation in services trade. Meanwhile, strengthening people-to-people exchanges will help enhance mutual understanding and act as a lubricant to resolving China-EU trade conflicts and consolidating the China-EU comprehensive strategic partnership, Song said. Economic globalization has made the interests of China and the EU increasingly inseparable, weaving their economies into a deeply complementary whole that sustains prosperity for both and for the world at large. In 2025, China-EU trade in goods exceeded $800 billion, with their combined economic output accounting for more than one-third of the global total, bilateral trade volume making up nearly one-quarter of the world's total, and nearly half of bilateral trade consisting of intermediate goods.

item.title: German president's first day of visit in Anhui highlights Germany's 'dual-track' approach to China: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28 17:36:00
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier visits the Volkswagen Group China Technology Company (VCTC) and tries a vehicle associated with CARIZON, a company specializing in advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), on October 27, 2026. Photo: Steinmeier's Instagram account "Essentially, China's first opening-up to the West took place here," German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier wrote in an Instagram post on Tuesday after completing the first day of his visit in Hefei, capital of East China's Anhui Province. His itinerary included a visit to the former residence of Li Hongzhang, a tour of an urban water management system and a stop at a major Volkswagen research and development center, reflecting a willingness to gain a deeper understanding of China in the complex context of China-Germany relations, a Chinese expert said. In a post titled "History, Urban Development and E-Mobility," accompanied by 19 Instagram Stories documenting the first day of his visit, Steinmeier said he began his China trip in Hefei, visiting the former residence of late Qing Dynasty statesman Li, who met Otto von Bismarck in Germany in 1896, and Luogang Central Park, a former airport site featuring a water management system to prevent flooding and improve the urban climate. He ended the day at Volkswagen Group China Technology Company (VCTC), the automaker's largest R&D center outside Germany, which focuses on electric mobility. "Relations between Germany and China are so diverse that they do not fit into a simple black-and-white pattern," Steinmeier said. He noted that his visit would therefore extend beyond economic hotspots and deliberately take a broader view of China. Anhui was a fitting choice, he said, "because, essentially, China's first opening-up to the West took place here." The choice of Hefei as the first stop of the visit is noteworthy, as it offers a perspective on China that goes beyond high-level meetings and symbolic diplomatic engagements, Feng Zhongping, director of the Institute of European Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times. The itinerary reflects an effort to gain a deeper understanding of China through its history, culture and economic development, sending a positive signal that Germany is willing to better understand the country amid the complexities of current China-Germany relations, Feng said. The expert noted that Germany is increasingly seeking to maintain economic ties with China while protecting its own industries, reflecting a dual-track approach to bilateral relations. Photos accompanying the post also showed Steinmeier himself trying out a vehicle associated with CARIZON, a company that specializes in advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and autonomous driving technologies. The automotive industry is a pillar of Germany's economy, and the rapid development of electric vehicles has made cooperation with China increasingly important for German companies. While European countries remain concerned about competition and the protection of domestic industries, they also recognize that China is an indispensable partner in tackling shared challenges, Feng added. Ahead of the visit, Steinmeier said on social media on Monday that the trip would focus on Germany's multifaceted relationship with China and the challenges facing the two countries. In an earlier Instagram post outlining his visit to Anhui, Steinmeier said that in Beijing, the second stop of his visit, the program includes talks with Chinese leaders and a speech at Peking University on China's role in the world. On Friday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a regular press conference that the sound and steady growth of the comprehensive strategic partnership between China and Germany, the world's second- and third-largest economies, not only serves the interests of both countries, but is also what Europe and the world hope to see. "We hope to work with the German side to take this visit as an opportunity to cement mutual trust, deepen cooperation and seek joint innovation, so as to make greater progress in bilateral relations, contribute to steady and sustained growth of China-Europe relations, and bring fresh energy to the world," Mao added. German media outlet DW described the state visit as taking place "in uncertain times," noting that Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region while also seeking to maintain good ties with Beijing. The Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) similarly noted that bilateral relations are "diverse but also complex," while trade ties are being recalibrated. The Europe-China Forum 2026, scheduled for November 5, will address these questions. According to the organizers, the issue is not only how Europe and China can manage their differences, but also how they can build a relationship capable of navigating global transitions together over the next 50 years. Steinmeier's visit comes as European countries continue to consider how to manage relations with China amid economic interdependence and strategic differences. The challenge is not simply whether to cooperate with China, but how to sustain engagement while addressing trade disputes and concerns over market competition, Feng said.
